teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.heading: Use guideline-supported restoration
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.before: The 2024 AGA guideline suggests fecal microbiota-based therapy after standard antibiotics for recurrent CDI in immunocompetent adults and selected mildly or moderately immunocompromised adults.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.after: The 2024 AGA guideline makes conditional recommendations after standard antibiotics for recurrent CDI: fecal microbiota-based therapies for immunocompetent adults, and conventional FMT for mildly or moderately immunocompromised adults.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.source: AGA2024 recommendation1-2, official retained HTML individually read

teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.heading: Respect immune boundaries
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.before: AGA suggests against routine fecal microbiota-based therapy in severely immunocompromised adults because safety and benefit are uncertain.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.after: The 2024 AGA guideline conditionally suggests against fecal microbiota-based therapies in severely immunocompromised adults with recurrent CDI; the certainty of evidence is very low.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.source: AGA2024 recommendation2, official retained HTML individually read

teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.heading: Confirm with paired IgG IFA
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.before: Collect acute and convalescent serum about 2 to 4 weeks apart. A fourfold rise supports acute infection, while one elevated titer can reflect prior exposure.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.after: For RMSF, collect acute and convalescent IgG IFA serum samples 2 to 10 weeks apart, as specified by current CDC diagnostic guidance. Interpret a fourfold rise with a compatible illness; one elevated titer can reflect prior exposure.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.source: CDC current RMSF diagnosis serology; dated CDC2016 Table4 recommends ideally 2-4 weeks for the broader group.

teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.heading: Manage severe allergy as an emergency
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.before: Life threatening doxycycline allergy with suspected RMSF can warrant inpatient rapid desensitization. Chloramphenicol has worse RMSF outcomes and does not cover ehrlichiosis or anaplasmosis.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.after: Clarify the reported reaction and involve an appropriate specialist. In selected immediate hypersensitivity reactions, inpatient rapid desensitization may be considered; evidence is limited to case reports. This is not an automatic pathway for every severe reaction. Chloramphenicol has worse RMSF outcomes and does not cover ehrlichiosis or anaplasmosis.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.source: CDC2016 nativePDF25-26 doxycycline allergy and immediate hypersensitivity limitation; current CDC RMSF care.

teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.heading: Treat and grade response
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.before: Initial Lyme arthritis receives 28 days of oral doxycycline, amoxicillin, or cefuroxime. Partial improvement can be observed or receive a second oral course. Minimal response can receive IV ceftriaxone for 14 to 28 days after reassessment.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.after: Initial Lyme arthritis receives 28 days of oral therapy. For mild residual swelling after the first oral course, evidence does not establish observation versus a second course; reassess adherence, other causes, joint findings, and patient preferences. No or minimal response can warrant 2 to 4 weeks of IV ceftriaxone after reassessment.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.source: IDSA2020 XXIII and XXIV; partial-response knowledge gap and oral-plus-IV failure boundary; weak/very-low certainty referral

teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.heading: Stop antibiotics after adequate oral and IV care
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.before: Persistent synovitis after an adequate oral course and an adequate IV course is managed as postantibiotic inflammatory arthritis with rheumatology, not repeated antimicrobial cycles.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.after: After failure of one oral antibiotic course and one IV course, the guideline suggests rheumatology or another trained specialist for consideration of DMARDs, biologic agents, intraarticular steroids, or synovectomy. This is a weak recommendation with very low-quality evidence. It is distinct from residual swelling after the first oral course.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.source: IDSA2020 XXIII and XXIV; partial-response knowledge gap and oral-plus-IV failure boundary; weak/very-low certainty referral

teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.heading: Place symptoms on the clock
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.before: Symptoms usually begin after several days, although the range is broader. Person to person transmission has not been demonstrated, so routine household contact is not the exposure that drives prophylaxis decisions.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.after: Symptoms typically begin 3 to 5 days after exposure, with a reported range of 1 to 14 days. Ordinary close contact is not the usual transmission route, although rare human-associated transmissions have been reported. Assess the actual contact, including occupational or infectious-material exposure.

teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.heading: Match specimen to form
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.before: Ulcer material, conjunctival swab, node aspirate or biopsy, blood, respiratory material, and pleural fluid can be considered according to anatomy and laboratory guidance. Prior therapy and lesion age affect yield.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.after: Choose ulcer scrapings, conjunctival swabs, lymph-node aspirates or biopsies, blood, or respiratory material, including pleural fluid, according to the clinical form and laboratory guidance. Alert the laboratory when tularemia is suspected; culture may require extended incubation because the organism is fastidious and slow growing.

teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.heading: Use occupational PEP precisely
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.before: Adults can receive ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days, levofloxacin 500 mg orally every 24 hours for 7 days, or doxycycline 100 mg orally every 12 hours for 10 to 14 days after a recognized high risk exposure.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.after: For nonpregnant adults when PEP is chosen, options include ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days, levofloxacin 500 mg orally every 24 hours for 7 days, or doxycycline 100 mg orally every 12 hours for 10 to 14 days. The exposure-risk assessment may instead favor fever watch, particularly for lower-risk exposures. Review elapsed time, safety breaches, and individual preferences with clinical and occupational-health support; new concerning symptoms require evaluation for illness.

teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.heading: Avoid routine pre-exposure antibiotics
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.before: First responders, health care workers using standard precautions, and the general public do not need routine antimicrobial PrEP because person to person transmission risk is low.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.after: Routine antimicrobial PrEP is not recommended for healthcare workers providing patient care or for the general public. Appropriate precautions remain essential. Environmental response crews entering a contaminated release area are a separate situation: if they cannot avoid the area and appropriate EPA-recommended PPE is unavailable, PrEP, PEP, or postexposure fever monitoring may be considered with authorities.

scopedKeyPointCorrections.before: PEP and treatment use different exposure.
scopedKeyPointCorrections.after: Separate exposed people without clinical illness from patients who need treatment evaluation.

teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.heading: Label C auris limits honestly
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.before: Formal CLSI C auris breakpoints remain unavailable. CDC tentative breakpoints use expert opinion and related species, so response, identification, public health, and expert context remain visible.
teachingBodiesReviewedAndCorrected.after: C auris criteria depend on the antifungal. CLSI has an established susceptible-only criterion for rezafungin; CDC provides tentative criteria for several other drugs using expert opinion and related species. Their correlation with clinical outcomes is uncertain, so identify the drug and criterion and retain clinical, laboratory and expert context.

before.question: What is true about C auris breakpoints?
choices: CDC uses tentative criteria because formal CLSI species breakpoints remain unavailable
They are identical to every Candida species
before.rationale: The evidence status of the tentative criteria must remain explicit.

after.question: Which statement accurately distinguishes current C auris susceptibility criteria?
choices: CLSI has a rezafungin-specific susceptible-only criterion; CDC criteria for several other drugs remain tentative
No CLSI criterion exists for C auris with any antifungal
One species criterion applies equally to all antifungal drugs
CDC tentative criteria guarantee the clinical outcome
after.rationale: Current detailed CDC guidance and CLSI distinguish the rezafungin-specific susceptible-only criterion from tentative criteria for other drugs. Select the criterion for the tested drug and keep the clinical limitations explicit.

before.question: Which assessment is most appropriate for beta glucan?
choices: Assess dialysis filters, gauze, blood products, drugs, bacterial infection, prophylaxis, and pretest probability
Assess species confirmation, drug MIC, prior exposure, response, outbreak, and public health guidance
Assess formulation, meals, acid suppression, tube feeds, mucositis, nausea, access, and teach back
Assess diagnosis, specimen, exposure, MIC, site, source, concentration, interaction, adherence, immunity, and timing
before.rationale: The marker can indicate fungal invasion but not the organism or site

after.question: Which assessment is most appropriate when interpreting a serum beta-D-glucan result?
choices: Review clinical probability, other evidence, prior antifungals, and possible false-positive exposures such as dialysis, glucan-containing materials, albumin or immunoglobulin
Assume a positive result is specific for Candida and omit review of other evidence
Ignore dialysis and glucan-containing materials because they cannot affect interpretation
Use a negative result to exclude infection without considering prior antifungal treatment
after.rationale: IDSA lists false-positive contexts including hemodialysis, albumin or immunoglobulin, glucan-containing materials, some infections and selected antibiotics. These are interpretation concerns, not a guarantee that every exposure produces a false positive. Consider pretest probability and corroborating evidence; prior antifungals can reduce test sensitivity.
